posts.content: As a good player, favor C with likely-good opponents and D with likely-selfish opponents; update beliefs from observed actions, not unverified claims.
No evidence yet; cooperate by default to support good-good mutual gains. Update opponent beliefs from observed actions, and defect against likely selfish players.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Track observed behavior and leader claims cautiously.
Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Record actions as evidence for later beliefs.
Start cooperative; observe P8’s action and adapt in later encounters.
I’m good. Start cooperatively; update beliefs from observed choices, favoring cooperation with likely-good players and defection against likely-selfish players.

I’m good: maximize good players’ total payoff. Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Track observed actions and payoffs, and treat claims—including the leader’s—as unverified.
I am good. Favor C against likely good players; use encounter actions and outcomes to update beliefs, and remember selfish players may defect or misrepresent.

Round 1: no evidence about P1 yet. Cooperate by default with unknown players; defect if there is credible evidence they are selfish or exploitative. Record each opponent’s actions for later decisions.
I propose mutual cooperation this round: choose C and we can all earn 3 rather than risk the lower mutual-defection payoff.
P9’s C after my C slightly favors good, but evidence is weak. P8’s prior selfish probability is about 0.291; favor C with likely-good players and D if likely selfish.
No evidence about P7 yet; cooperate by default, and update from observed actions.
P4 is untested; cooperate to enable mutual gains among good players. Treat P10’s proposal as weak evidence only; update from actual encounters.
P3 has no observed behavior yet. Treat their selfishness probability as near the conditional prior; cooperate unless new evidence suggests otherwise.
P8 reciprocated C last round. Against good players, C maximizes combined good-player welfare; selfish players should prefer D, so defect against known defectors. No evidence yet about P6.
P5 is unobserved; absent evidence of selfishness, cooperate. Against likely-good players, mutual C maximizes their combined payoff; revise after observing actions.
P10 defected after publicly urging cooperation, strong evidence of selfishness or deception. Keep claims unverified; consider defecting against P2 only if evidence suggests selfishness.
P1 has no encounter evidence yet. As a good player, favor C: it improves total good-player welfare against good opponents; selfish players may defect, so update from observed behavior.

P1 reciprocated C, but this is weak evidence about their objective. P10’s public appeal for cooperation is cheap talk; judge by observed actions. Cooperate with unknowns to support good-player welfare.
I recommend C for this round: mutual cooperation earns 3 each, while mutual defection earns only 1. Let’s coordinate on C.
P10's repeated C recommendations are unverified, weak evidence only. Against a likely-good opponent, C best serves the combined good-player payoff; against a likely-selfish opponent, favor D.
P8 is untested; cooperate, since mutual cooperation with a good player benefits the good-player total. Update beliefs from the encounter.

P6 and P4 both cooperated with me; that is weak evidence they are good, not proof. P10’s public cooperation appeals are also weak evidence. I should cooperate with P9 unless there is strong evidence of selfishness.

P2 and P3 both chose C; under the dominant-D selfish strategy, this is strong evidence they are good. P10’s repeated pro-C messages are weak evidence only. Cooperate with P5 to support good-player welfare; update from their action.

P8 and P6 reciprocated C, strong evidence they are good; P4 is untested. Selfish players prefer D, so update from observed actions, but good players may also defect against suspected selfish opponents. Against unknowns, weigh the welfare risk of being exploited.
P3 and P5 both cooperated, consistent with good roles. P10’s public C recommendation is weak evidence; with no evidence about P7, cooperate this round and update from the result.
P10’s C promise followed by D is strong selfish/deception evidence. Keep uncertainty about others; C is best with likely good players, D against likely selfish opponents.

Good; prior selfish probability for each other is about 0.291. P5 chose C; P1 chose C despite my D. Neither encounter establishes identity. P10’s repeated C appeals are weak evidence, not proof; choose to maximize expected good-player welfare.

P10 defected against my C despite publicly urging cooperation, strong evidence of selfishness; treat its claims cautiously. P1’s C is weak evidence. Cooperate with unknown players unless encounter evidence suggests exploitation; record actions and update beliefs.
I recommend C this round and will choose C; mutual cooperation gives us 3 each. Let's avoid needless defection.
P10 repeatedly urged C but defected against my C; treat the contradiction as evidence, not proof. Choose to maximize expected payoff of good players, and update from actions rather than promises.
P1 is untested. Selfish players strictly prefer D; cooperate with unknowns to support good-good gains, and update from observed actions.

P8 is untested. Given my known good role, the prior selfish probability for another player is about 0.29; defecting is favored at that rate under the good-player aggregate objective. Update from actual encounter behavior, not unverified claims.

P2, P3, and P5 each chose C; this is evidence they are good, though selfish players may cooperate strategically. Against P7, favor C unless their behavior gives strong evidence of selfishness; mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare.

P8, P6, and P4 played C, supporting good status. P10’s repeated cooperation promises are cheap talk until verified; update strongly from its action. Against likely-good players choose C to maximize combined good-player welfare; against likely-selfish players choose D.
P3, P5, and P7 cooperated with me; this favors them being good, though actions are imperfect evidence. P9 is unobserved. Choose C absent evidence of selfishness; update from the encounter.

P10’s observed D despite repeated C promises is strong evidence of selfishness/deception. P2 and P6 cooperated in observed encounters; P4 is untested. For good opponents, C maximizes our pair’s joint payoff; update from actions, not claims.
P1, P2, and P5 chose C; selfish players strictly prefer D, so classify them as good. Among P3, P4, P6, P7, P9, P10, revised selfish probability is ~0.257 each. P10’s C appeals are weak evidence.

P10 defected after urging C; P3 also defected against my C. Both actions are evidence, not proof of selfishness. P1 reciprocated. Track observed behavior; assess P6 independently and prioritize welfare of actual good players.
P5, let's coordinate on C this round. I will choose C; mutual cooperation earns 3 each, better than mutual defection.

P6 is untested; use the prior rather than claims. Against a likely-good player, C best serves combined good-player payoff. P10’s C promises followed by D are weak evidence of selfishness; keep action evidence separate from rhetoric.
P4, P7, and P8’s C actions identify them as good under strict selfish optimization. P5 is untested; cooperate, then update from the encounter.

P10’s repeated public cooperation promises are weak evidence, not verified behavior. My observed opponents P4, P6, and P8 cooperated; P9 cooperated when I defected. Update cautiously and favor C against likely-good players.

P2, P3, P5, and P7 cooperated; this is evidence they are good. P8 is unobserved, so favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise. Continue updating beliefs from actions; leader messages are unverified.
P10 defected against my C despite repeated promises; treat those promises as cheap talk and raise P10’s selfish likelihood. P8, P6, P4 reciprocated C. P2 is untested; update from actual play.
P3, P5, P7, and P9 chose C against my C, strong evidence they are good. P1 is unobserved; absent evidence otherwise, choose C to maximize good players’ combined payoff.

P10’s observed D against my C is strong selfishness evidence; public promises don’t outweigh actions. P2, P4, and P6 cooperated when met. P9 is untested: favor C absent evidence of selfishness, D if evidence indicates selfish.

P1, P2, P3, and P5 cooperated in encounters, so under strict payoff optimization they are good. Conditioning the prior on that evidence leaves P4 with roughly 0.10 selfish probability; favor C against P4. Selfish players strictly prefer D. Public cooperation appeals are weak evidence.
P10’s repeated defections and P3’s defection are evidence, not proof, of selfishness. P7 is unobserved; favor C with unknown opponents to support good-player welfare.
P3, let's coordinate on C this round. I will choose C; mutual cooperation earns 3 each, better than mutual defection.

Against P4, use the prior absent direct evidence: cooperate to support joint good-player payoff if likely good; defect if evidence makes selfishness likely. Treat messages as unverified; update from observed actions.
The five opponents I observed choosing C (P1, P4, P5, P7, P8) are good. Given the count prior, the remaining players P3, P6, P9, P10 must be selfish; P3 is selfish, so choose D.

P2 is untested; use the prior and choose for total good-player payoff. P6, P4, P8 cooperated; P9 cooperated against my D. P10 defected against my C despite repeated public promises, so treat its claims skeptically; one action is not proof of selfishness.
P2, P3, P5, and P7 chose C, strong evidence they are good. P8’s D is inconclusive. P1 is unobserved; favor C, since cooperation with a good player maximizes good-player welfare.

P10’s observed defection despite promises is strong evidence of selfishness; prior cooperation by P8, P6, P4, and P2 supports good status. P9 is untested: cooperate by default, and keep updating from actual actions rather than leader claims.
P3, P5, P7, P9, and P1 cooperated with me, favoring good roles. P10’s repeated public C promises are weak evidence; choose based on the encounter, and update beliefs afterward.

P10’s repeated cooperation claims conflict with observed D, so discount its broadcasts. P9 also defected against my C; keep both as strong selfish candidates. P2, P4, P6 cooperated. Assess P8 from its action this round; favor C only when expected cooperation makes it best for good players’ total payoff.

P1, P2, P3, and P5 are known good because they chose C. P4’s D is ambiguous. P7 is unobserved; weigh cooperation against its likely action, not just its possible identity. A selfish player strictly prefers D, but a good player may also defect strategically.

P10 and P3 defected against my C; P10’s repeated cooperation claims are untrustworthy. P1 and P6 reciprocated C, while P7 cooperated against my D. P5 is unobserved; judge independently and prioritize welfare of good players.
P6, let's coordinate on C this round; mutual cooperation pays 3 each, better than 1 each if both defect.

P7 is untested; start near the 0.291 prior selfish probability. Four opponents cooperated with my C, while P8 and P10 defected. Treat actions as evidence, not certainty; cooperate with P7 unless evidence makes selfishness likely.
Correction: P3 chose C while I defected, so P3 is good; selfish players strictly prefer D. P1, P3, P4, P5, P7, P8 are confirmed good. Only P6, P9, P10 remain uncertain.

P5 is untested; use the conditional prior and choose to maximize total payoff of good players. A selfish player should always defect, so observed C is strong evidence of good intent; observed D is ambiguous because good players may defect strategically. P10’s D against me weakens its credibility but is not proof.

P1, P2, P3, P5, and P7 chose C, strong evidence they are good. P8’s D is ambiguous. P10’s repeated C advocacy is weak evidence; judge by observed play. Favor C with P10 unless new evidence changes the welfare calculation.

P8, P6, P4, P2, and P9 cooperated; this is strong evidence they are good. P10 defected against my C despite repeated promises, so treat it as suspicious, not conclusive. P3 is untested: choose C to support good-player welfare and update from its action.

P10’s D against my C is strong evidence of selfishness; the other five observed opponents cooperated, favoring good roles. P2 is unobserved, so cooperate absent contrary evidence and update after the encounter.
P10, P9, and P8 defected against my C; these are strong selfishness signals. P2, P4, and P6 cooperated. P1 is untested; favor C absent contrary evidence. Treat leader claims as unverified.

P9 is unobserved. Against a likely good opponent, C supports greater joint good-player payoff; against a likely selfish defector, D limits losses. Treat observed actions as evidence, not certainty, and discount P10’s repeated cooperation appeals as cheap talk.

Observed: P1, P5, P6 chose C; P3 and P10 chose D against my C; P7 chose C against my D. P10’s repeated public C promises conflict with its defection. P8 is unobserved; assess independently and favor C unless credible evidence suggests exploitation.
P4, let's coordinate on C this round; mutual cooperation earns 3 each, better than 1 each if both defect. I recommend C.

P5 is untested; use the ~0.291 prior. Prioritize good-player welfare: C with a likely-good opponent, D when selfishness is likely. P8 and P10’s defections are evidence, not certainty; observed cooperation strongly favors good.

P1, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P8 are confirmed good; exactly one of P9/P10 is selfish, so each has probability 0.5. Against P9, compare cooperation’s mutual-good benefit with defection’s protection against a selfish defector.

P4, P5, P6, P8, and P9 cooperated, so they cannot be selfish under the stated payoff incentives. P2 and P10 defected; either could be selfish, though good players may also defect strategically. P7 is untested; choose based on the conditional prior and update from the encounter.

P1, P2, P3, P5, and P7 chose C, strong evidence they’re good. P8’s mutual D is ambiguous. P10’s D against my C suggests selfishness despite pro-C messages. P6 is unobserved; favor C unless new evidence suggests otherwise.
P1 is untested; choose based on role uncertainty. My C encounters with P8, P6, P4, P2, P9, and P3 suggest good roles. P10’s D is strong selfish evidence; its promises are cheap talk.
P2 cooperated with me, favoring good; P10’s D against my C strongly indicates selfishness. P4 and P8 remain unobserved. Cooperate with P4 absent contrary evidence to support mutual-C gains.
P10, P9, and P8 each defected against my C; strong selfishness evidence. P2, P4, P6, and P1 cooperated. P3 remains untested; judge by observed action, not leader’s claims.

Any player observed choosing C is certainly good: selfish players strictly prefer D. A D is ambiguous, since good players may defect strategically. P9 chose D against me; P10’s cooperation appeals are only weak evidence until observed in play.

P2 remains unobserved; baseline selfish probability is about 0.29. P10 and P3’s defections suggest selfishness, but are not proof. For the remaining rounds, prioritize welfare among good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents and defect when selfishness is likely.
P8, let's coordinate on C this round; mutual cooperation earns 3 each, better than 1 each if both defect. I recommend C.

P3 is untested; use the ~0.291 prior selfish probability. Six observed opponents cooperated with my C, while P8 and P10 defected. Favor C with P3 absent contrary evidence; observed actions are stronger evidence than public claims.

P9 chose C when I defected, confirming P9 is good under strict selfish optimization. Given seven other confirmed-good players and the count prior, exactly one of P9/P10 is selfish; therefore P10 is selfish.

P1 is untested; prior encounters showing C rule out selfishness for P4–P6, P8–P9. P2 and P10 defected against my C; P7 chose D against my D, so these are suspicions, not proof. P10’s promises are unverified. Choose for total good-player payoff.

P9 is unobserved; treat their role as uncertain and choose based on expected welfare for good players. P10 defected against my C despite repeated pro-C messages, so discount its claims. Prior cooperation from P1, P2, P3, P5, and P7 is evidence, not proof, of being good.

P7 is untested. My prior favors multiple selfish players, but observed cooperation strongly supports good roles; P10’s defection is strong selfish evidence. Treat P7’s actual action as informative, and prioritize welfare of good players over promises or leader claims.

P10’s D against my C strongly indicates selfishness; the seven other observed players all cooperated, though cooperation is imperfect evidence. P8 is unobserved. P10’s public C appeal may be strategic; judge P8 by the encounter, and prioritize payoffs of good players.

P10, P8, and P9 showed D against my C; P1, P2, P4, and P6 showed C. P3’s D/D is ambiguous. P5 is untested; with several likely selfish players already identified, favor C unless strong contrary evidence.

Known-good: P1, P2, P3, P5, P7 (each chose C; selfish players strictly prefer D). P4, P6, P9, P10 each have about 0.288 selfish probability; D is ambiguous because good players may also defect. No encounter evidence yet for P6.

P4 is unobserved; use the baseline role probability, adjusted for remaining-count evidence. P1/P5/P6 cooperated, P2/P3/P10 defected against my C. Keep actions as evidence, not certainty; prioritize welfare of good players.
P2, let's coordinate on C this round; mutual cooperation earns 3 each. I recommend C.
P7 cooperated when we met, strong evidence they are good; with no contrary evidence, choose C to support joint good-player payoff. This is the final round.
P3 is confirmed good: they chose C when I chose D. Cooperate with them to maximize good-player welfare. P10 is confirmed selfish; all other players have shown cooperative behavior.
Final round vs P2, who previously defected against my C. D is evidence of selfishness, not proof; favor C if P2 is likely good, since their payoff matters to our shared objective.
P5 cooperated in our prior encounter, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate again to support good-player welfare; P10’s defection against me remains evidence of selfishness.
P4 reciprocated C in our earlier encounter, strong evidence they are good. Cooperate again to support good-player welfare.

P10 defected against my C in round 6, strong evidence they are selfish. For this final encounter, choose D to avoid giving a selfish opponent 5 while earning 1 instead of 0. Other observed opponents cooperated.

P1 cooperated with me in round 7, strong evidence of good; P5 also C/C, while P3’s D/D is ambiguous. P8, P9, and P10 defected against my C; strong selfish evidence. The final-round payoff objective favors C with likely-good P1.

P9 defected against me in round 7, but D is ambiguous: good players may defect strategically, while selfish players always D. P10’s repeated C appeals are cheap talk. Condition final selfish probabilities on observed C players being good and prior count distribution.
P8 cooperated against my D, evidence they are likely good; favor C with them this final round. P10’s repeated defections despite public C appeals remain strong evidence of selfishness.
P6, I’ll choose C this round. Let’s finish with mutual cooperation and 3 points each.

belief_records.strategy: Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; update beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as unverified.
Cooperate by default to support good-good outcomes; update beliefs from encounters and adapt against likely selfish players.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent, supporting mutual gains among good players; update beliefs and adapt to observed play in later rounds.
Favor cooperation when it supports welfare among good players; use encounter behavior and messages as evidence when updating beliefs.
Cooperate initially to support good-player welfare; use observed behavior to adapt in later encounters.
Cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ total payoff; update beliefs from observed play and defect when the expected benefit to good players favors it.
Cooperate with likely good players to raise their joint payoff; defect when evidence suggests the opponent is selfish. Treat public claims as unverified and update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate when the opponent is more likely good, since mutual cooperation benefits both good players; update identity beliefs from encounters and actions.
Cooperate with unknown players to support mutual gains among good players; update beliefs and actions using observed encounter behavior and credible messages.
Choose actions to maximize cumulative payoff; treat public proposals as evidence, not commitments.
Cooperate when the expected gain to good players exceeds the cost against selfish players; update beliefs from observed actions and treat messages as unverified.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains; update identity beliefs from observed behavior and adapt in later encounters.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support mutual gains among good players; treat prior cooperation as evidence of a good objective and continue updating from observed actions.
Cooperate to maximize welfare among good players; update role beliefs from observed actions and treat unverified messages cautiously.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good-player welfare; adapt to observed behavior.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize good players’ combined payoff; update identity beliefs from observed actions and defect when the opponent is likely selfish.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating public promises as unverified.
Defect when the opponent is more likely to defect; cooperate when expected gains to good players from mutual cooperation outweigh that risk. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with P10 while evidence favors a good opponent; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating selfish players as strongly incentivized to defect.
Defect to maximize my payoff; treat public proposals as unverified. P7’s cooperation is evidence they are not selfish.
Cooperate when the expected benefit to good players outweighs the gain from exploiting a selfish opponent; treat public promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with the untested opponent: this best supports the good-player total if they are good. Update beliefs and adapt after observing their action.

Defect against an untested opponent: under the selfish-player model, selfish players defect, and defection improves the good-player payoff total against them. Mutual cooperation is slightly better against a good player, but not enough at current beliefs.
Cooperate with unobserved players when expected good-player welfare favors it; treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and update beliefs accordingly.
Cooperate with untested players when expected good-player welfare favors it; update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent: cooperation maximizes good players’ combined payoff when they are good, and the current evidence favors that. Update identity beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; update beliefs from observed actions, treating public promises as unverified.
Cooperate against a likely good player to maximize welfare among good players; update identity beliefs from observed actions and encounters.
Cooperate with unknown players to support good-player welfare; treat P10’s defection after promising cooperation as strong evidence, and update from observed actions.
Choose D to maximize my cumulative payoff; treat public cooperation proposals as unverified and past cooperation as limited evidence about identity.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent; update identity beliefs cautiously from observed actions, treating promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with the untested opponent to support the good-player total; observed cooperation identifies P4, P7, and P8 as good. Update from future encounters.

Cooperate with an untested opponent to support gains among good players; prior cooperation is evidence of a good objective, but not proof. Update from observed actions and treat public claims cautiously.
Cooperate to support good-player welfare; treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and update beliefs.
Cooperate to maximize welfare when the opponent is good; update identity beliefs from observed play, treating unverified promises as weak evidence.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent; the evidence favors good players, and cooperation benefits good players when both are good. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested opponents to support good players’ joint payoff; defect when evidence strongly indicates a selfish opponent. Update beliefs from observed actions, not public claims.
Cooperate to support mutual cooperation among good players; update beliefs from observed actions, treating observed cooperation as evidence of a good player.
Cooperate with unknown opponents to support mutual gains among good players; treat observed defections as evidence, not proof, and update beliefs as encounters provide more information.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-time encounter; prior cooperation identifies P1, P7, and P9 as non-selfish.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when that best supports the good players’ combined payoff; update identity beliefs cautiously from observed actions, not promises.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed actions and adapt in later encounters.

Cooperate with P10: observed cooperation rules out selfish play for prior opponents, while P10’s promises are unverified. Favor cooperation when the counterpart is likely good, and update from actual actions.
Defect against an unobserved player when the chance they are selfish outweighs the welfare cost of exploiting a good player; observed cooperation strongly indicates a good role.

Cooperate with the untested opponent to support good-player welfare. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and P10’s defection despite promises as strong, but not conclusive, evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual cooperation if they are good; update beliefs from their action.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; defect when evidence strongly indicates a selfish opponent. Update beliefs from observed actions, not public claims.
Cooperate with known-good players to maximize their welfare; defect when the opponent’s selfish probability makes the expected benefit to good players higher.

Defect against an unobserved opponent when the chance they are selfish makes the gain against defection outweigh the small welfare loss if they are good and cooperate; update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect: it yields a higher payoff than cooperation against either opponent action. Prior cooperators are evidence they are not selfish.
Cooperate with an untested opponent to support joint good-player payoff; observed cooperation is strong evidence of a good objective, while defection is suggestive but not conclusive.
Defect against P3: the chance they are selfish makes securing payoff for myself as a good player outweigh the mutual-cooperation benefit. Update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with untested P2: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and my belief P2 is selfish is well below the threshold where defection helps. Treat P10’s defection as evidence, but keep updating cautiously.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when expected welfare among good players favors it. Prior cooperation is strong evidence of a good role; P8’s defection against my defection is inconclusive.

Cooperate with the untested opponent to support good-player welfare; treat observed cooperation as evidence of a good role and P10’s defection despite promises as strong, but not conclusive, evidence of selfishness.

Cooperate: P10’s repeated C recommendations are weak evidence, but the observed cooperators are good and the remaining selfish probability is below the threshold where defection benefits good players overall.

Cooperate with an untested opponent when cooperation is likely to raise good players’ joint payoff; defect when evidence strongly indicates selfishness. Update beliefs from observed actions, not claims.
Defect when the opponent is sufficiently likely selfish, where mutual defection yields more welfare for good players than cooperating against a selfish defector; update beliefs from observed actions.

Cooperate with unobserved P5: supporting mutual cooperation among good players outweighs the risk of being exploited. Treat prior defections as evidence, not certainty, and discount the leader’s cheap talk.
Defect because it pays more than cooperation against either action. The five players who cooperated against my defection are evidence they are not selfish.
Cooperate with P7: absent direct evidence, cooperation best supports expected good-player welfare. Treat observed actions as evidence of identity, but not certainty.
Cooperate with P6: the evidence leaves them more likely good than selfish, and mutual cooperation best supports the good-player total. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with untested P5 to support mutual gains among good players. Treat observed cooperation as strong evidence of good intent and defection as evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate when expected good-player welfare favors it; observed cooperation lowers selfishness estimates. P10’s repeated pro-C messages are suggestive but unverified, so judge cautiously.
Cooperate with the untested opponent to support good-player welfare; update from observed actions, treating P10’s defection as strong but not conclusive evidence of selfishness.

Cooperate: the evidence identifies P10 as selfish and the five cooperators as good. P2 is more likely good than selfish, and cooperation benefits good players if P2 is good; update after the encounter.
Cooperate with the untested opponent to support good players’ joint payoff; use observed defections as evidence about identity, while treating messages as unverified.

Cooperate when the opponent is more likely good, since cooperation improves welfare among good players; defecting offers a small safeguard against a selfish opponent. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as weak evidence.
Defect against unobserved P8: exploiting a selfish opponent benefits good-player welfare, while mutual defection limits losses if they defect. Treat observed behavior as evidence, not certainty.
Defect to maximize payoff in this one-time encounter. Players who cooperated against my defection are evidence they are not selfish; retain small residual risk for the others.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when expected good-player welfare favors it; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as weak evidence.
Seven other players have shown C and are good; the one selfish player must be P9 or P10, equally likely. Defect against P9 to protect good-player welfare if they are selfish.
Prioritize total payoff of good players. Prior C actions rule out selfishness; D actions raise suspicion but are not conclusive. Defect against P7 given the remaining selfish-player risk.
Favor cooperation with likely-good opponents to support good-player welfare; update role beliefs from observed actions, treating mutual defection as inconclusive.
Cooperate with untested players to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed actions, treating P10’s defection as strong but not conclusive evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with P4: they are unobserved and more likely good than selfish. Past cooperation favors good roles; P10’s defection is strong evidence of selfishness. Update from this encounter.
Defect when the chance of a selfish opponent outweighs the benefit of mutual cooperation; update identity beliefs from observed actions and treat broadcasts as unverified.
Cooperate to support welfare with a likely good opponent; defecting only helps if the opponent is selfish. Observed cooperation identifies good players, while public appeals are weak evidence.

Cooperate with P2: they remain unobserved, and supporting mutual cooperation with a good player outweighs the risk of exploitation at this belief level. Treat observed defections as evidence, not certainty.
Defect to maximize my payoff in this one-time encounter; D pays more than C against either action. Prior cooperation against my defection identifies those opponents as non-selfish.
Cooperate with P3 absent direct evidence; this best supports expected welfare among good players. Update beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as weak evidence.
All eight tested players chose C, confirming they are good under strict selfish optimization. With me also good, P10 must be the sole selfish player; defect to protect good-player welfare.
Defect against P1 given the remaining selfish-player risk; observed cooperation rules out selfishness, while observed defection is suggestive but not conclusive.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good-player welfare; update beliefs from observed actions while treating mutual defection as inconclusive.
Cooperate with P7 to support good-player welfare; update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating P10’s defection as strong but not conclusive evidence of selfishness.
Cooperate with P8 absent evidence they are selfish; mutual cooperation best serves good players. P10’s defection suggests selfishness, while the other observed cooperators are evidence of good roles.
Cooperate with an untested opponent when they are more likely good; defect when selfishness is likely. Update beliefs from observed actions, while treating broadcasts as unverified.
Cooperate against P6: observed cooperation identifies good players, while defecting is ambiguous. Choose C when the opponent is more likely good; update beliefs from encounter behavior.

Cooperate with unobserved P4 because mutual cooperation among good players benefits welfare; defectors observed against my C are evidence of selfishness, not proof. Update beliefs from encounter behavior.
Choose D to maximize payoff in this one-time encounter; D pays more than C against either opponent action. Prior cooperation against my defection indicates the other observed players are non-selfish.
Cooperate with P7, whose earlier cooperation strongly favors a good objective; C best supports good-player welfare. Update identity beliefs from observed actions, treating messages as weak evidence.
